# Amazon Route 53: questions

## Worked examples

<!-- quiz:start id=route53-q001 -->
### Question 1

A company hosts the DNS records for its domain, example.com, in an Amazon Route 53 public hosted zone. The company's website runs on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The marketing team wants users to open the website by typing example.com in a browser, without the www prefix. The DNS answer for example.com must keep working when the load balancer scales. Which DNS record should a solutions architect create in the hosted zone to meet these requirements?

- A CNAME record for example.com whose value is the DNS name of the Application Load Balancer.
- An alias record of type A for example.com that points to the Application Load Balancer.
- An A record for example.com whose value is the current IP addresses of the Application Load Balancer.
- An NS record for example.com whose value is the DNS name of the Application Load Balancer.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** An alias record of type A for example.com that points to the Application Load Balancer.

**Deciding phrases.** "without the www prefix", "behind an Application Load Balancer", "must keep working when the load balancer scales"

**Think aloud.**

1. I read the last sentence first: it asks for the DNS record that meets these requirements.
2. I mark the constraints: the name is example.com without www, the target is an Application Load Balancer, and the answer must keep working when the load balancer scales.
3. Before I look at the options, I predict a CNAME record to the DNS name of the load balancer, because a CNAME record maps one name to another name.
4. I remove the A record with the current IP addresses, because the load balancer changes its addresses as it scales. I remove the NS record, because an NS record names the name servers of a hosted zone, not a website.
5. Between the CNAME record and the alias record the difference is where the record sits; the stem says example.com, with no www. My first idea breaks because example.com is the zone apex, where the DNS protocol does not allow a CNAME record.
6. Check: the alias record of type A sits at the zone apex, points to the load balancer and follows its address changes. Time: 90 seconds.

**Why.** The name example.com is the zone apex, [the top node of a DNS namespace](../facts/route53.md#route53-alias-allowed-at-zone-apex). An alias record to a load balancer works [both for the root domain](../facts/route53.md#route53-elb-alias-record-for-root-and-subdomains) and for subdomains. Route 53 supports alias records for [three types of load balancers](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-apex-alias-elb-three-types), and the Application Load Balancer is one of them.

**Why not.**

- "A CNAME record for example.com whose value is ...": The [DNS protocol does not allow you to create](../facts/route53.md#route53-cname-dns-protocol-forbids-zone-apex) a CNAME record at the zone apex, and example.com is the apex.
- "An A record for example.com whose value is ...": Elastic Load Balancing scales the load balancer and its DNS entry has a [time-to-live (TTL) of 60 seconds](../facts/route53.md#route53-elb-dns-entry-updated-ttl-60), so copied addresses go stale.
- "An NS record for example.com whose value is ...": An NS record [identifies the name servers for the hosted zone](../facts/route53.md#route53-ns-record-identifies-name-servers); it delegates a domain and does not point a name to a load balancer.

**Twin.** If the stem said "users open www.example.com" instead: a CNAME record would also resolve, because the rule that blocks it applies [for the top node of a DNS namespace](../facts/route53.md#route53-cname-dns-protocol-forbids-zone-apex), not for subdomains.

**Takeaway.** At the zone apex, use an alias record for an AWS resource; a CNAME record fits subdomains such as www.

**Review.** [An alias record can answer at the zone apex where a CNAME record cannot](2-deep.md#an-alias-record-can-answer-at-the-zone-apex-where-a-cname-record-cannot-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 2

A company will migrate www.example.com from web servers in its data center to an Application Load Balancer next Saturday. In the Route 53 public hosted zone, www.example.com is an A record with a TTL of 86,400 seconds. Users must move to the new site with minimal downtime, and the team must be able to roll back quickly if the new site fails. Which approach will meet these requirements with the LEAST downtime for users?

- On Saturday, replace the A record with an alias record for the load balancer, because Route 53 sends record changes to all of its servers within a minute.
- Two days before Saturday, lower the TTL of the A record to 300 seconds; on Saturday, replace the record with an alias record for the load balancer.
- On Saturday, lower the TTL of the A record to 300 seconds and replace it with an alias record for the load balancer in the same change.
- Create a second public hosted zone for example.com with an alias record for the load balancer, and change the name servers at the registrar on Saturday.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Two days before Saturday, lower the TTL of the A record to 300 seconds; on Saturday, replace the record with an alias record for the load balancer.

**Deciding phrases.** "a TTL of 86,400 seconds", "minimal downtime", "roll back quickly", "LEAST downtime"

**Think aloud.**

1. I read the last sentence first: it asks for the approach with the LEAST downtime for users.
2. I mark the constraints: the A record has a TTL of 86,400 seconds, the move is next Saturday, and the team must be able to roll back quickly.
3. Before I look at the options, I predict that the TTL must go down days before the move, because resolvers keep a cached answer until its TTL runs out.
4. I remove the change on Saturday alone, because Route 53 updates its own servers fast, but resolvers keep the old answer for up to a day. I remove the second hosted zone, because resolvers also cache NS records, typically for two days.
5. Between lowering the TTL two days early and lowering it on Saturday, the difference is when the caches learn the short TTL; the stem says minimal downtime, so the short TTL must be in every cache before Saturday.
6. Check: lowering the TTL two days early meets every constraint, and a roll back also reaches users within minutes. Time: 90 seconds.

**Why.** Resolvers cache an answer [according to their time to live (TTL)](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-resolver-caches-by-ttl-outside-control), so after a change some users keep the old address for up to 86,400 seconds. Lower the TTL first, as AWS advises: [temporarily shorten the TTLs](../facts/route53.md#route53-best-practice-shorten-ttl-before-critical-change). After two days every cache holds the short TTL, so the switch and a roll back reach users within minutes.

**Why not.**

- "On Saturday, replace the A record with an ...": Route 53 updates its own servers [within 60 seconds](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-propagation-within-60-seconds), but resolvers keep the old answer until the TTL of 86,400 seconds runs out.
- "On Saturday, lower the TTL of the A ...": Resolvers that cached the old answer keep it for the old TTL of 86,400 seconds, so a lower TTL set on Saturday comes too late.
- "Create a second public hosted zone for example.com ...": Resolvers cache NS records too, with a typical TTL of [172800 seconds](../facts/route53.md#route53-ns-record-typical-ttl-172800), so a change of name servers moves users more slowly.

**Twin.** If the stem said "an A record with a TTL of 60 seconds" instead: change the record on Saturday, because resolvers cache the old answer [according to their time to live (TTL)](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-resolver-caches-by-ttl-outside-control).

**Takeaway.** Lower the TTL before a planned DNS change, and wait for the old TTL to pass before the switch.

**Review.** [Resolvers cache each answer for its TTL before they ask Route 53 again](2-deep.md#resolvers-cache-each-answer-for-its-ttl-before-they-ask-route-53-again-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 3

A company runs a web application in the us-east-1 Region and keeps a static maintenance page in an Amazon S3 bucket that is configured as a website. The company creates Amazon Route 53 failover records for www.example.com. The primary record is an alias record for an Application Load Balancer. The secondary record points to the S3 website endpoint. The company must ensure that Route 53 sends users to the maintenance page when the application cannot serve requests. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create a Route 53 health check that sends HTTP requests to the primary endpoint, and associate the health check with the primary record.
- Run a scheduled AWS Lambda function that tests the application every minute and repoints the primary record to the S3 website endpoint on failure.
- Turn on Evaluate Target Health for the primary record, so that Route 53 uses the health of the resource that the record points to.
- Create a Route 53 health check of the S3 website endpoint, and associate the health check with the secondary record.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Turn on Evaluate Target Health for the primary record, so that Route 53 uses the health of the resource that the record points to.

**Deciding phrases.** "The primary record is an alias record for an Application Load Balancer", "when the application cannot serve requests", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Route 53 [responds to DNS queries using the primary record](../facts/route53.md#route53-failover-one-primary-one-secondary-responds-secondary-when-unhealthy) when the primary is healthy, so the primary needs a health signal. This primary is an alias record for a load balancer. Setting Evaluate Target Health lets Route 53 [route traffic away from unhealthy resources](../facts/route53.md#route53-evaluate-target-health-benefit-for-elb-beanstalk), with no health check to create or pay for.

**Why not.**

- "Create a Route 53 health check that sends ...": It works, but AWS says to [associate health checks only with non-alias records](../facts/route53.md#route53-health-check-alias-record-not-recommended); this alias record can take its health from the load balancer.
- "Run a scheduled AWS Lambda function that tests ...": It works, but it adds code to run and record edits, and AWS calls such edits [a non-statically-stable design](../facts/route53.md#route53-fi-record-edits-depend-on-control-plane).
- "Create a Route 53 health check of the ...": Route 53 [responds to DNS queries using the secondary record](../facts/route53.md#route53-failover-one-primary-one-secondary-responds-secondary-when-unhealthy) when the primary is unhealthy, so a check on the secondary does not detect the application failure.

**Twin.** If the stem said "an A record with the Elastic IP address of one EC2 instance" instead: a Route 53 health check on the primary, because instances need a [record and a health check for each resource](../facts/route53.md#route53-simple-config-alias-targets-no-health-check-needed).

**Takeaway.** Failover primary that is an alias record for a load balancer: turn on Evaluate Target Health, not a separate health check.

**Review.** [Failover records answer with the secondary only while the primary is unhealthy](2-deep.md#failover-records-answer-with-the-secondary-only-while-the-primary-is-unhealthy-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 4

A company runs the same stateless web application in us-east-1 and eu-west-1, behind an Application Load Balancer in each Region. The application has users around the world. The company hosts its DNS records in a Route 53 public hosted zone. Each user must be served from the Region that gives that user the lowest latency. Which routing configuration for www.example.com will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Latency alias records for the two load balancers, one record in each Region, with Evaluate Target Health turned on for both records.
- Geolocation alias records: a Europe record that points to the eu-west-1 load balancer, and a Default record for the us-east-1 load balancer.
- Weighted alias records for the two load balancers with equal weights, so that each Region receives half of the DNS queries for the name.
- IP-based records with a CIDR collection that the team keeps current with the client IP ranges that each of the two Regions must serve.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Latency alias records for the two load balancers, one record in each Region, with Evaluate Target Health turned on for both records.

**Deciding phrases.** "Each user must be served from the Region that gives that user the lowest latency", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The requirement names latency, not a place. Latency records send each user to [the Region that provides the best latency](../facts/route53.md#route53-choose-latency-routing-best-latency-region), with no list of networks to maintain. Evaluate Target Health lets Route 53 [route traffic away from unhealthy resources](../facts/route53.md#route53-evaluate-target-health-benefit-for-elb-beanstalk) if one Region fails.

**Why not.**

- "Geolocation alias records: a Europe record that points ...": Geolocation routing uses the [geographic location of the requests](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-geo-vs-latency-geography-not-latency), and in some cases geography is not a good proxy for latency.
- "Weighted alias records for the two load balancers ...": Weights split queries among [multiple resources in proportions that you specify](../facts/route53.md#route53-choose-weighted-routing-proportions), whatever the location of the user, so half of the users reach the slower Region.
- "IP-based records with a CIDR collection that the ...": It can work, but the team maintains the client IP ranges by hand; IP-based routing suits users [from certain ISPs to specific endpoints](../facts/route53.md#route53-ip-based-routing-use-cases).

**Twin.** If the stem said "Because of a data residency rule, users in Europe must be served from eu-west-1, and all other users from us-east-1" instead: geolocation records, because each user location [always goes to the same endpoint](../facts/route53.md#route53-geolocation-use-cases).

**Takeaway.** Lowest latency for each user means latency records; a rule about places means geolocation records.

**Review.** [Latency records follow measured latency and geolocation records follow user location](2-deep.md#latency-records-follow-measured-latency-and-geolocation-records-follow-user-location-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 5

A company serves its website at the edge through an Amazon CloudFront distribution. IPv6 is turned on for the distribution, and example.com is an alternate domain name of the distribution. The company hosts example.com in an Amazon Route 53 public hosted zone. Users on IPv4 networks and users on IPv6 networks must reach the website at example.com. Which combination of actions should the company take in the hosted zone to meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

- Create a CNAME record for example.com whose value is the domain name of the CloudFront distribution.
- Create an alias record of type A for example.com that points to the domain name of the CloudFront distribution.
- Create an A record for example.com that lists the IP addresses that the distribution's domain name returns today.
- Create a Lambda function that rewrites A and AAAA records for example.com with the distribution's addresses every minute.
- Create an alias record of type AAAA for example.com that points to the domain name of the CloudFront distribution.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- Create an alias record of type A for example.com that points to the domain name of the CloudFront distribution.
- Create an alias record of type AAAA for example.com that points to the domain name of the CloudFront distribution.

**Deciding phrases.** "IPv6 is turned on for the distribution", "Users on IPv4 networks and users on IPv6 networks", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Example.com is the zone apex, and an alias record can map it to [your Amazon CloudFront distribution](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-apex-alias-cloudfront). With IPv6 turned on, you [create two records](../facts/route53.md#route53-alias-cloudfront-ipv6-two-records): type A for IPv4 and type AAAA for IPv6.

- With IPv6 turned on, you [create two records](../facts/route53.md#route53-alias-cloudfront-ipv6-two-records) for the distribution; this alias record of type A answers the IPv4 users.
- An AAAA record routes traffic [using an IPv6 address](../facts/route53.md#route53-aaaa-record-ipv6), so this alias record serves the IPv6 users of the distribution.

**Why not.**

- "Create a CNAME record for example.com whose value ...": The [DNS protocol does not allow you to create](../facts/route53.md#route53-cname-dns-protocol-forbids-zone-apex) a CNAME record at the zone apex, and example.com is the apex.
- "Create an A record for example.com that lists ...": CloudFront addresses [vary based on your end user’s location](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-cloudfront-ip-addresses-vary-by-location) and can change, so a fixed list sends users to wrong edges.
- "Create a Lambda function that rewrites A and ...": It adds code to run, and it copies addresses that [vary based on your end user’s location](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-cloudfront-ip-addresses-vary-by-location); alias records need no upkeep.

**Twin.** If the stem said "IPv6 is turned off for the distribution" instead: the alias record of type A is enough, because the AAAA record routes [using an IPv6 address](../facts/route53.md#route53-aaaa-record-ipv6).

**Takeaway.** Apex of a CloudFront site with IPv6: two alias records, type A and type AAAA.

**Review.** [An alias record follows the changing addresses of the AWS resource it names](2-deep.md#an-alias-record-follows-the-changing-addresses-of-the-aws-resource-it-names-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 6

A company registered the domain example.com with a third-party registrar, which also hosts the DNS records today. The company wants to migrate the DNS service for example.com to Amazon Route 53. Because of a contract, the domain registration must stay with the current registrar. Users on the internet must keep resolving the company's website during the change. What should the company do?

- Transfer the domain registration to Route 53 first, then create the records in the hosted zone that Route 53 creates for the domain.
- Create a Route 53 private hosted zone with the records, and associate the hosted zone with the VPC that runs the website.
- Create a Route 53 public hosted zone with the records, then change the domain's name servers at the registrar to the hosted zone's name servers.
- Create the records in Route 53, and add a CNAME record at the registrar that points example.com to a Route 53 name server.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create a Route 53 public hosted zone with the records, then change the domain's name servers at the registrar to the hosted zone's name servers.

**Deciding phrases.** "the domain registration must stay with the current registrar", "migrate the DNS service", "Users on the internet"

**Why.** If the registrar does not use the name servers of the hosted zone, Route 53 [will not be authoritative for queries](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-registrar-must-use-hosted-zone-name-servers) to the domain. So the company copies the records into a public hosted zone first, and then changes the name servers at the current registrar. A transfer of the registration is optional.

**Why not.**

- "Transfer the domain registration to Route 53 first, ...": A transfer is possible, but [this isn't required to use other Route 53 features](../facts/route53.md#route53-domain-transfer-not-required-for-other-features), and the contract keeps the registration where it is.
- "Create a Route 53 private hosted zone with ...": A private hosted zone will [only return these records when queried from within](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-private-zone-answers-only-from-associated-vpcs) associated VPCs, so internet users get no answers.
- "Create the records in Route 53, and add ...": The [DNS protocol does not allow you to create](../facts/route53.md#route53-cname-dns-protocol-forbids-zone-apex) a CNAME record at example.com, and delegation names name servers, not a CNAME target.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the company also wants Route 53 as its registrar" instead: transfer the registration too, because [you can transfer the domain registration to Route 53](../facts/route53.md#route53-domain-transfer-not-required-for-other-features).

**Takeaway.** Keep the registrar, move the DNS: create a public hosted zone and change the name servers at the registrar.

**Review.** [A resolver follows the delegation to the name servers of your hosted zone](2-deep.md#a-resolver-follows-the-delegation-to-the-name-servers-of-your-hosted-zone-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 7

A company runs a web application in the us-east-1 Region and keeps a static maintenance page in an Amazon S3 bucket that is configured as a website. The company creates Amazon Route 53 failover records for www.example.com. The primary record is an A record with the Elastic IP address of one EC2 instance. The secondary record points to the S3 website endpoint. The company must ensure that Route 53 sends users to the maintenance page when the application cannot serve requests. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create a Route 53 health check that sends HTTP requests to the primary endpoint, and associate the health check with the primary record.
- Run a scheduled AWS Lambda function that tests the application every minute and repoints the primary record to the S3 website endpoint on failure.
- Turn on Evaluate Target Health for the primary record, so that Route 53 uses the health of the resource that the record points to.
- Create a Route 53 health check of the S3 website endpoint, and associate the health check with the secondary record.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create a Route 53 health check that sends HTTP requests to the primary endpoint, and associate the health check with the primary record.

**Deciding phrases.** "The primary record is an A record with the Elastic IP address of one EC2 instance", "when the application cannot serve requests", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Route 53 [responds to DNS queries using the primary record](../facts/route53.md#route53-failover-one-primary-one-secondary-responds-secondary-when-unhealthy) when the primary is healthy, so the primary needs a health signal. An A record with an Elastic IP address names no AWS resource whose health Route 53 can read. A Route 53 health check of the instance gives that signal, and a failing check sends users to the S3 maintenance page.

**Why not.**

- "Run a scheduled AWS Lambda function that tests ...": It works, but it adds code to run and record edits, and AWS calls such edits [a non-statically-stable design](../facts/route53.md#route53-fi-record-edits-depend-on-control-plane).
- "Turn on Evaluate Target Health for the primary ...": Evaluate Target Health decides [whether Route 53 checks the health of the resource](../facts/route53.md#route53-evaluate-target-health-other-policies-checks-resource) that an alias record refers to; this A record is not an alias record.
- "Create a Route 53 health check of the ...": Route 53 [responds to DNS queries using the secondary record](../facts/route53.md#route53-failover-one-primary-one-secondary-responds-secondary-when-unhealthy) when the primary is unhealthy, so a check on the secondary does not detect the application failure.

**Twin.** If the stem said "an alias record for an Application Load Balancer" instead: turn on Evaluate Target Health, because for that alias record you [set Evaluate Target Health to Yes](../facts/route53.md#route53-alias-to-aws-use-evaluate-target-health-not-health-check).

**Takeaway.** A failover primary that points to an EC2 instance needs its own Route 53 health check.

**Review.** [Failover records answer with the secondary only while the primary is unhealthy](2-deep.md#failover-records-answer-with-the-secondary-only-while-the-primary-is-unhealthy-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 8

A company runs the same stateless web application in us-east-1 and eu-west-1, behind an Application Load Balancer in each Region. The application has users around the world. The company hosts its DNS records in a Route 53 public hosted zone. Because of a data residency rule, users in Europe must be served from eu-west-1, and all other users from us-east-1. Which routing configuration for www.example.com will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Latency alias records for the two load balancers, one record in each Region, with Evaluate Target Health turned on for both records.
- Geolocation alias records: a Europe record that points to the eu-west-1 load balancer, and a Default record for the us-east-1 load balancer.
- Weighted alias records for the two load balancers with equal weights, so that each Region receives half of the DNS queries for the name.
- IP-based records with a CIDR collection that the team keeps current with the client IP ranges that each of the two Regions must serve.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Geolocation alias records: a Europe record that points to the eu-west-1 load balancer, and a Default record for the us-east-1 load balancer.

**Deciding phrases.** "data residency rule", "users in Europe must be served from eu-west-1", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** A data residency rule ties a place to a Region, so the location of the user decides. Geolocation routing sends traffic [based on the location of your users](../facts/route53.md#route53-choose-geolocation-routing-user-location), and the Default record [handles both queries from unmapped IP addresses](../facts/route53.md#route53-geolocation-default-record-handles-unmapped) and the queries from places outside Europe.

**Why not.**

- "Latency alias records for the two load balancers, ...": Latency-based routing uses [latency data taken over a period of time](../facts/route53.md#route53-latency-changes-over-time), so a European user can reach us-east-1 when that Region measures faster for the user.
- "Weighted alias records for the two load balancers ...": Weights split queries among [multiple resources in proportions that you specify](../facts/route53.md#route53-choose-weighted-routing-proportions), whatever the location of the user, so half of the European users reach us-east-1.
- "IP-based records with a CIDR collection that the ...": It can work, but the team maintains the client IP ranges of Europe by hand; IP-based routing suits users [from certain ISPs to specific endpoints](../facts/route53.md#route53-ip-based-routing-use-cases).

**Twin.** If the stem said "Each user must be served from the Region that gives that user the lowest latency" instead: latency records, because they route traffic to [the Region that provides the best latency](../facts/route53.md#route53-choose-latency-routing-best-latency-region).

**Takeaway.** A rule about where users are served is a geolocation question, with a Default record for everyone else.

**Review.** [Latency records follow measured latency and geolocation records follow user location](2-deep.md#latency-records-follow-measured-latency-and-geolocation-records-follow-user-location-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 9

A company runs its own DNS servers for its public domain on two Amazon EC2 instances in one Availability Zone of the us-east-1 Region. The DNS servers answer queries from customers on the internet. The company wants a fully managed DNS service that keeps answering queries if an Availability Zone or a whole AWS Region fails. What should a solutions architect recommend?

- Move the DNS servers to EC2 instances in two Availability Zones of us-east-1, behind a Network Load Balancer.
- Create a Route 53 private hosted zone for the domain, and associate it with VPCs in two AWS Regions.
- Create inbound Resolver endpoints in two Availability Zones of us-east-1, and send the internet DNS queries to the endpoint addresses.
- Create a Route 53 public hosted zone for the domain, and update the domain's name servers at the registrar.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create a Route 53 public hosted zone for the domain, and update the domain's name servers at the registrar.

**Deciding phrases.** "fully managed DNS service", "if an Availability Zone or a whole AWS Region fails", "customers on the internet"

**Why.** Public and private DNS in Route 53 are [all global services](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-route53-still-global-service), answered by a [global anycast network of DNS servers](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-global-anycast-low-latency). The loss of one zone or one Region does not stop the answers. The registrar has to use the zone's name servers, or Route 53 [will not be authoritative for queries](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-registrar-must-use-hosted-zone-name-servers).

**Why not.**

- "Move the DNS servers to EC2 instances in ...": Two Availability Zones survive a zone failure, but every server still sits in us-east-1, and the company still runs the DNS software itself.
- "Create a Route 53 private hosted zone for ...": A private hosted zone will [only return these records when queried from within](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-private-zone-answers-only-from-associated-vpcs) the associated VPCs, so internet customers get no answers.
- "Create inbound Resolver endpoints in two Availability Zones ...": [VPC Resolver is a Regional service](../facts/route53.md#route53-vpc-resolver-regional) that answers queries that reach a VPC; it does not host a public domain for internet users.

**Twin.** If the stem said "names that only instances in its VPCs resolve" instead: a private hosted zone, which will [only return these records when queried from within](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-private-zone-answers-only-from-associated-vpcs) associated VPCs.

**Takeaway.** Public DNS that survives a zone or Region failure: a Route 53 public hosted zone.

**Review.** [A resolver follows the delegation to the name servers of your hosted zone](2-deep.md#a-resolver-follows-the-delegation-to-the-name-servers-of-your-hosted-zone-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

## Extended

<!-- quiz:start id=route53-q005 -->
### Question 10

A company has a hybrid network. Its data center connects to a VPC in the eu-west-1 Region through an AWS Direct Connect dedicated connection. The VPC is associated with an Amazon Route 53 private hosted zone named corp.internal. DNS servers in the data center host the zone onprem.corp. Servers in the data center must resolve names in corp.internal. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create an outbound Resolver endpoint and a forwarding rule for onprem.corp that targets the data center DNS servers, and associate the rule with the VPC.
- Run DNS forwarder software on EC2 instances in two Availability Zones, and configure both networks to forward queries for the other zone to them.
- Create an inbound Resolver endpoint in the VPC, and configure the data center DNS servers to forward corp.internal queries to the endpoint's IP addresses.
- Configure the data center DNS servers to forward corp.internal queries to the VPC Resolver address at the base of the VPC CIDR range plus two.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create an inbound Resolver endpoint in the VPC, and configure the data center DNS servers to forward corp.internal queries to the endpoint's IP addresses.

**Deciding phrases.** "Servers in the data center must resolve names in corp.internal", "private hosted zone named corp.internal", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The queries start in the data center and need answers from the private hosted zone, so they travel into the VPC. Inbound endpoints carry queries [from your on-premises network or another VPC](../facts/route53.md#route53-resolver-inbound-endpoint-definition), and Route 53 VPC Resolver answers them from corp.internal. AWS names [conditional forwarding rules and Resolver endpoints](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-vpc-resolver-hybrid-forwarding-direct-connect-vpn) as the way to resolve names across Direct Connect.

**Why not.**

- "Create an outbound Resolver endpoint and a forwarding ...": [Outbound Resolver endpoints allow DNS queries](../facts/route53.md#route53-resolver-outbound-endpoint-definition) from the VPC to the data center, which is the opposite direction: onprem.corp names for the VPC.
- "Run DNS forwarder software on EC2 instances in ...": It works, but endpoints and rules forward queries [without having to deploy additional DNS servers](../facts/route53.md#route53-hybrid-resolver-endpoints-no-extra-dns-servers), so forwarder instances add patching and scaling work.
- "Configure the data center DNS servers to forward ...": Forwarding from on-premises DNS servers to the CIDR+2 address [is not supported, and can cause unstable results](../facts/route53.md#route53-resolver-cidr-plus-two-forwarding-unsupported).

**Twin.** If the stem said "EC2 instances in the VPC must resolve names in onprem.corp" instead: an outbound endpoint and a forwarding rule, because [Outbound Resolver endpoints allow DNS queries](../facts/route53.md#route53-resolver-outbound-endpoint-definition) out of the VPC.

**Takeaway.** Data center asks the VPC: inbound endpoint. VPC asks the data center: outbound endpoint and a forwarding rule.

**Review.** [Resolver endpoints carry DNS queries between a VPC and an on-premises network](2-deep.md#resolver-endpoints-carry-dns-queries-between-a-vpc-and-an-on-premises-network-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=route53-q013 -->
### Question 11

A company runs a web application behind an Application Load Balancer in us-east-1 and keeps a warm standby copy behind another Application Load Balancer in us-west-2. Amazon Route 53 hosts the company's public DNS records. The cross-Region recovery plan must move users to us-west-2 when the application in us-east-1 fails, even if the Route 53 control plane is impaired during the event. Which combination of steps will make the plan the MOST resilient? (Select TWO.)

- During the event, change the weights of weighted alias records so that the us-west-2 load balancer gets all the traffic.
- Create failover alias records in advance, with the us-east-1 load balancer as the primary and the us-west-2 load balancer as the secondary.
- During the event, create a new record that points the application's domain name to the us-west-2 load balancer.
- Base the health of the primary record on a health check or on Evaluate Target Health, so that Route 53 fails over by itself.
- Before the event, move the hosted zone from us-east-1 to us-west-2 so that DNS changes can be made in us-west-2.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- Create failover alias records in advance, with the us-east-1 load balancer as the primary and the us-west-2 load balancer as the secondary.
- Base the health of the primary record on a health check or on Evaluate Target Health, so that Route 53 fails over by itself.

**Deciding phrases.** "even if the Route 53 control plane is impaired during the event", "move users to us-west-2", "MOST resilient"

**Why.** AWS says [you should not rely on the Route 53 control plane in your recovery path](../facts/route53.md#route53-fi-no-control-plane-in-recovery-path). In an impairment, DNS answers and health checks [will continue to work](../facts/route53.md#route53-fi-impairment-dns-and-health-checks-keep-working). So the records exist before the event, and health status moves the users.

- AWS says to [pre-provision resources that require DNS records](../facts/route53.md#route53-fi-preprovision-for-multi-region-dr), so no record change is needed during the event.
- Health-based failover is a [highly reliable operation done on the data plane](../facts/route53.md#route53-dr-health-check-failover-data-plane), so no person must act during the event.

**Why not.**

- "During the event, change the weights of weighted ...": It works only when the control plane works: [this is a control plane operation](../facts/route53.md#route53-dr-weight-change-is-control-plane), so it is less resilient.
- "During the event, create a new record that ...": Creating records to fail over is [a non-statically-stable design](../facts/route53.md#route53-fi-record-edits-depend-on-control-plane), because it depends on the control plane.
- "Before the event, move the hosted zone from ...": Public DNS, private DNS and health checks in Route 53 are [all global services](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-route53-still-global-service), so a hosted zone has no Region to move to.

**Twin.** If the stem said "an operator must approve each failover" instead: keep the failover records and switch them with ARC routing control; AWS recommends [features like Route 53 health checks and ARC routing control that rely on data plane functionality](../facts/route53.md#route53-bp-control-plane-prioritizes-consistency-not-availability).

**Takeaway.** Create failover records before the event and let health status move users; record edits need the control plane.

**Review.** [DNS answers and health check failover keep working when the control plane is impaired](2-deep.md#dns-answers-and-health-check-failover-keep-working-when-the-control-plane-is-impaired-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=route53-q021 -->
### Question 12

A small team runs version 1 of a web application behind one Application Load Balancer. The team deploys version 2 behind a second Application Load Balancer in the same Region. The team wants about 10 percent of users to reach version 2 first, a larger share during the next week, and a quick way to send every user back to version 1 if errors appear. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create failover alias records with the version 1 load balancer as the primary and the version 2 load balancer as the secondary.
- Create weighted alias records for the two load balancers with weights of 90 and 10, and change the weights to shift users or roll back.
- Create multivalue answer alias records for the two load balancers, and change how many records each version has to shift users.
- Run a scheduled script that switches a simple alias record between the two load balancers to approximate the share of users.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create weighted alias records for the two load balancers with weights of 90 and 10, and change the weights to shift users or roll back.

**Deciding phrases.** "about 10 percent of users to reach version 2 first", "send every user back to version 1", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** AWS names weighted routing for [testing new versions of software](../facts/route53.md#route53-choose-weighted-routing-proportions). Route 53 answers in the [ratio of a resource's weight to the total](../facts/route53.md#route53-weighted-ratio-of-weight-to-total), so weights of 90 and 10 send about one DNS query in ten to version 2. A higher version 2 weight shifts more users, and a weight of zero on version 2 sends everyone back.

**Why not.**

- "Create failover alias records with the version 1 ...": Route 53 answers with the secondary [when the first one is unhealthy](../facts/route53.md#route53-failover-routing-primary-or-secondary), so version 2 gets no users when version 1 works.
- "Create multivalue answer alias records for the two ...": Multivalue answer alias records are [not supported](../facts/route53.md#route53-multivalue-alias-not-supported) in Route 53, so the load balancers cannot be targets of this routing policy.
- "Run a scheduled script that switches a simple ...": It needs code, a schedule and monitoring, but weighted routing sends traffic to [multiple resources in proportions that you specify](../facts/route53.md#route53-choose-weighted-routing-proportions) without them.

**Twin.** If the stem said "version 2 receives users only when version 1 fails" instead: failover alias records, because the secondary answers [when the first one is unhealthy](../facts/route53.md#route53-failover-routing-primary-or-secondary).

**Takeaway.** Share users between versions with weighted records; a weight of zero takes one version out.

**Review.** [Weighted records give each resource its share of the total weight](2-deep.md#weighted-records-give-each-resource-its-share-of-the-total-weight-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=route53-q012 -->
### Question 13

A company uses failover records in a Route 53 private hosted zone for an internal API. The primary record is an A record for the API, which runs on Amazon EC2 instances that have only private IP addresses. The secondary record points to a standby copy of the API. Route 53 must fail over to the secondary record when the primary API stops working. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements in the MOST secure way? (Select TWO.)

- Create an Amazon CloudWatch metric that reflects the health of the primary API, and create a CloudWatch alarm that watches that metric.
- Create a Route 53 HTTP health check that sends requests to the private IP address of one primary instance, and associate it with the primary record.
- Add the IP ranges of the Route 53 health checkers to the security group of the primary instances, so that the health checkers can reach the API.
- Create a Route 53 health check that monitors the state of the CloudWatch alarm, and associate that health check with the primary record.
- Assign public IP addresses to the primary instances, allow the health checker IP ranges in their security group, and check those public addresses.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- Create an Amazon CloudWatch metric that reflects the health of the primary API, and create a CloudWatch alarm that watches that metric.
- Create a Route 53 health check that monitors the state of the CloudWatch alarm, and associate that health check with the primary record.

**Deciding phrases.** "private hosted zone", "have only private IP addresses", "when the primary API stops working", "MOST secure"

**Why.** Route 53 [health checkers are outside the VPC](../facts/route53.md#route53-hc-checkers-outside-vpc-need-public-ip), so they cannot reach a private address. For instances with only private IP addresses, AWS documents three steps: create a [CloudWatch metric, associate an alarm with the metric](../facts/route53.md#route53-hc-private-endpoint-cloudwatch-alarm-health-check), and then create a health check [based on the data stream for the alarm](../facts/route53.md#route53-hc-private-endpoint-cloudwatch-alarm-health-check).

- The metric and its alarm judge the API from inside AWS, so the instances need no public address and no inbound path.
- A health check [based on the data stream for the alarm](../facts/route53.md#route53-hc-private-endpoint-cloudwatch-alarm-health-check) turns unhealthy with the alarm, and Route 53 then answers with the secondary record.

**Why not.**

- "Create a Route 53 HTTP health check that ...": [Route 53 cannot check the health of endpoints](../facts/route53.md#route53-hc-cannot-check-private-ip-ranges) whose IP address is in [local, private, nonroutable, or multicast ranges](../facts/route53.md#route53-hc-cannot-check-private-ip-ranges).
- "Add the IP ranges of the Route 53 ...": The [health checkers are outside the VPC](../facts/route53.md#route53-hc-checkers-outside-vpc-need-public-ip), so a security group rule gives them no path to instances that have no public IP address.
- "Assign public IP addresses to the primary instances, ...": It works, because for an IP check you [must assign a public IP address](../facts/route53.md#route53-hc-checkers-outside-vpc-need-public-ip), but public addresses expose the API, which the alarm-based check avoids.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the primary record is an alias record for an internal Application Load Balancer" instead: for that resource AWS says to [set Evaluate Target Health to Yes](../facts/route53.md#route53-alias-to-aws-use-evaluate-target-health-not-health-check) on the record.

**Takeaway.** For a private endpoint, base the Route 53 health check on a CloudWatch alarm, not on the private IP address.

**Review.** [Health checkers around the world decide whether an endpoint is healthy](2-deep.md#health-checkers-around-the-world-decide-whether-an-endpoint-is-healthy-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=route53-q011 -->
### Question 14

A company has a hybrid network. Its data center connects to a VPC in the eu-west-1 Region through an AWS Direct Connect dedicated connection. The VPC is associated with an Amazon Route 53 private hosted zone named corp.internal. DNS servers in the data center host the zone onprem.corp. EC2 instances in the VPC must resolve names in onprem.corp. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create an outbound Resolver endpoint and a forwarding rule for onprem.corp that targets the data center DNS servers, and associate the rule with the VPC.
- Run DNS forwarder software on EC2 instances in two Availability Zones, and configure both networks to forward queries for the other zone to them.
- Create an inbound Resolver endpoint in the VPC, and configure the data center DNS servers to forward corp.internal queries to the endpoint's IP addresses.
- Configure the data center DNS servers to forward corp.internal queries to the VPC Resolver address at the base of the VPC CIDR range plus two.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create an outbound Resolver endpoint and a forwarding rule for onprem.corp that targets the data center DNS servers, and associate the rule with the VPC.

**Deciding phrases.** "EC2 instances in the VPC must resolve names in onprem.corp", "DNS servers in the data center host the zone onprem.corp", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The queries start in the VPC and need answers from the data center DNS servers, so they travel out of the VPC. Outbound endpoints carry queries [from your VPC to your on-premises network](../facts/route53.md#route53-resolver-outbound-endpoint-definition). Resolver rules decide which queries go out and [which queries VPC Resolver answers itself](../facts/route53.md#route53-resolver-rules-control-forwarding), so a rule for onprem.corp sends only those names.

**Why not.**

- "Run DNS forwarder software on EC2 instances in ...": It works, but endpoints and rules forward queries [without having to deploy additional DNS servers](../facts/route53.md#route53-hybrid-resolver-endpoints-no-extra-dns-servers), so forwarder instances add patching and scaling work.
- "Create an inbound Resolver endpoint in the VPC, ...": [Inbound Resolver endpoints allow DNS queries](../facts/route53.md#route53-resolver-inbound-endpoint-definition) into the VPC from the data center, which is the opposite direction: corp.internal names for the data center.
- "Configure the data center DNS servers to forward ...": It serves corp.internal, not onprem.corp, and forwarding to the CIDR+2 address [is not supported, and can cause unstable results](../facts/route53.md#route53-resolver-cidr-plus-two-forwarding-unsupported).

**Twin.** If the stem said "Servers in the data center must resolve names in corp.internal" instead: an inbound endpoint, because [Inbound Resolver endpoints allow DNS queries](../facts/route53.md#route53-resolver-inbound-endpoint-definition) into the VPC.

**Takeaway.** VPC asks the data center: outbound endpoint and a forwarding rule. Data center asks the VPC: inbound endpoint.

**Review.** [Resolver endpoints carry DNS queries between a VPC and an on-premises network](2-deep.md#resolver-endpoints-carry-dns-queries-between-a-vpc-and-an-on-premises-network-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=route53-q018 -->
### Question 15

A company has a Route 53 public hosted zone for example.com with records for www.example.com and api.example.com. The company creates a private hosted zone named example.com, associates it with its production VPC, and adds a record for db.example.com. Currently, instances in the VPC resolve db.example.com but not api.example.com, so calls to the public API fail. The name db.example.com must stay private and must not change. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create api.example.com and the other public names that the instances use in the private hosted zone, with the same values as the public records.
- Set the VPC attributes enableDnsSupport and enableDnsHostnames to true, so that names missing from the private hosted zone are answered from the public hosted zone.
- Create an outbound Resolver endpoint and a forwarding rule for example.com that sends the DNS queries of the VPC to a public DNS resolver on the internet.
- Run DNS forwarder software on EC2 instances that answers db.example.com from a local zone file and forwards all other names to public DNS resolvers.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create api.example.com and the other public names that the instances use in the private hosted zone, with the same values as the public records.

**Deciding phrases.** "private hosted zone named example.com", "resolve db.example.com but not api.example.com", "must stay private and must not change", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** A private zone matches when it is a [parent of the domain name in the request](../facts/route53.md#route53-phz-parent-zone-counts-as-match), so example.com matches api.example.com. With no record for that name, Route 53 VPC Resolver [doesn't forward the request to a public DNS](../facts/route53.md#route53-matching-phz-no-record-returns-nxdomain) resolver. In split-view DNS, each zone needs its own records.

**Why not.**

- "Set the VPC attributes enableDnsSupport and enableDnsHostnames to ...": A matching private zone with no record for the name means [it returns NXDOMAIN (non-existent domain) to the client](../facts/route53.md#route53-matching-phz-no-record-returns-nxdomain), whatever the VPC attributes are.
- "Create an outbound Resolver endpoint and a forwarding ...": [The VPC Resolver rule takes precedence](../facts/route53.md#route53-resolver-rule-beats-phz-same-name) over the private zone [for the same domain name](../facts/route53.md#route53-resolver-rule-beats-phz-same-name), so db.example.com would go to public DNS and stop resolving.
- "Run DNS forwarder software on EC2 instances that ...": It works, but the team then runs, patches and scales the forwarder instances and keeps a second copy of db.example.com.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the private hosted zone is named db.example.com" instead: change nothing, because that zone is not a [parent of the domain name in the request](../facts/route53.md#route53-phz-parent-zone-counts-as-match) api.example.com.

**Takeaway.** A private hosted zone that matches a name hides the public zone of that name, so copy the public records you need.

**Review.** [A private hosted zone answers only through the VPC Resolver of its associated VPCs](2-deep.md#a-private-hosted-zone-answers-only-through-the-vpc-resolver-of-its-associated-vpcs-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=route53-q020 -->
### Question 16

An application runs in us-east-1 and ap-southeast-1 behind an Application Load Balancer in each Region. Both Regions must serve users at all times. Each user must reach the Region with the lowest latency, and users must leave a Region whose application fails. The company wants a highly available cross-Region design that the team can run with little effort. Which Route 53 configuration is the MOST operationally efficient?

- Failover alias records for the two load balancers, with us-east-1 as the primary, ap-southeast-1 as the secondary, and Evaluate Target Health turned on.
- Latency A records that hold the current IP addresses of each load balancer, with no health checks, because Route 53 skips a Region that stops answering.
- Latency alias records for the two load balancers, one record for each Region, with Evaluate Target Health set to Yes on both records.
- Latency alias records for the two load balancers, and a Route 53 HTTP health check of each load balancer that is associated with its record.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Latency alias records for the two load balancers, one record for each Region, with Evaluate Target Health set to Yes on both records.

**Deciding phrases.** "Both Regions must serve users at all times", "the Region with the lowest latency", "users must leave a Region whose application fails", "MOST operationally efficient"

**Why.** Both Regions active is active-active failover: [all the records that have the same name](../facts/route53.md#route53-active-active-failover-definition) stay active unless they are unhealthy. Latency records pick [the Region that provides the best latency](../facts/route53.md#route53-choose-latency-routing-best-latency-region), and [setting Evaluate target health to Yes](../facts/route53.md#route53-evaluate-target-health-benefit-for-elb-beanstalk) lets Route 53 [route traffic away from unhealthy resources](../facts/route53.md#route53-evaluate-target-health-benefit-for-elb-beanstalk) without extra health checks.

**Why not.**

- "Failover alias records for the two load balancers, ...": Route 53 [includes only the healthy primary resources](../facts/route53.md#route53-active-passive-only-healthy-primary-then-secondary), so ap-southeast-1 serves no users as long as us-east-1 is healthy.
- "Latency A records that hold the current IP ...": When a record has no health check, Route 53 [always considers it healthy](../facts/route53.md#route53-record-without-health-check-always-healthy), and the copied addresses go stale when the load balancer scales.
- "Latency alias records for the two load balancers, ...": It works, but for these resources AWS says to [set Evaluate Target Health to Yes](../facts/route53.md#route53-alias-to-aws-use-evaluate-target-health-not-health-check) instead of creating health checks to manage.

**Twin.** If the stem said "ap-southeast-1 must serve users only after us-east-1 fails" instead: failover alias records, because Route 53 then [begins to include only the healthy secondary resources](../facts/route53.md#route53-active-passive-only-healthy-primary-then-secondary) when the primary fails.

**Takeaway.** Active-active across Regions with the lowest latency: latency alias records with Evaluate Target Health on every record.

**Review.** [Route 53 leaves unhealthy records out of answers until every record is unhealthy](2-deep.md#route-53-leaves-unhealthy-records-out-of-answers-until-every-record-is-unhealthy-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=route53-q010 -->
### Question 17

A company runs a TCP service on six Amazon EC2 instances across two Availability Zones in one Region. Clients connect to service.example.com, which is in a Route 53 public hosted zone. New connections must be spread evenly across the healthy instances. When an instance fails, it must stop receiving new connections at once, also from clients that cached a DNS answer earlier. Which solution will provide a highly available design with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create a multivalue answer record for each instance under service.example.com, and associate a Route 53 health check with each of the six records.
- Run open-source proxy software on two EC2 instances in different Availability Zones to spread connections and check the six instances, with a record for each proxy.
- Create a Network Load Balancer with the six instances as targets in both Availability Zones, and an alias record for service.example.com that points to it.
- Create one simple A record for service.example.com that lists the IP addresses of all six instances, so that each client picks one address at random.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create a Network Load Balancer with the six instances as targets in both Availability Zones, and an alias record for service.example.com that points to it.

**Deciding phrases.** "spread evenly across the healthy instances", "also from clients that cached a DNS answer earlier", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** A Network Load Balancer spreads TCP connections across healthy targets, and when a target fails, [it stops routing traffic to that target](../facts/elb.md#elb-unhealthy-target-stop-resume). Clients connect to the load balancer, so an answer that a resolver cached [according to their time to live (TTL)](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-resolver-caches-by-ttl-outside-control) still leads to healthy instances.

**Why not.**

- "Create a multivalue answer record for each instance ...": Multivalue answer routing [returns only values for healthy resources](../facts/route53.md#route53-multivalue-purpose-not-lb-substitute), but [this isn't a substitute for a load balancer](../facts/route53.md#route53-multivalue-purpose-not-lb-substitute), and resolvers cache answers [according to their time to live (TTL)](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-resolver-caches-by-ttl-outside-control).
- "Run open-source proxy software on two EC2 instances ...": It works, but the proxy instances are software that the team patches, scales and monitors, which a managed load balancer avoids.
- "Create one simple A record for service.example.com that ...": Route 53 returns the values [to the recursive resolver in random order](../facts/route53.md#route53-simple-routing-multiple-values-random-order-no-health-check), and [they are not health checked](../facts/route53.md#route53-simple-routing-multiple-values-random-order-no-health-check), so clients keep picking failed instances.

**Twin.** If the stem said "clients need several healthy addresses and the company wants no load balancer" instead: multivalue answer records, because they return [up to eight healthy records](../facts/route53.md#route53-multivalue-up-to-eight-healthy).

**Takeaway.** Multivalue answer routing is not a load balancer; to take failed instances out at once, use Elastic Load Balancing.

**Review.** [Weighted records give each resource its share of the total weight](2-deep.md#weighted-records-give-each-resource-its-share-of-the-total-weight-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=route53-q022 -->
### Question 18

A company uses a shared-services account to centrally manage a private hosted zone named internal.example.com. One VPC in a separate workload account must resolve the records of that zone, and the records must stay private. In the Route 53 console of the shared-services account, an engineer tries to associate the zone with the workload VPC but cannot find the VPC. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create a VPC peering connection between a VPC in the shared-services account and the workload VPC, so that the workload VPC can query the private hosted zone.
- Authorize the association from the shared-services account with the AWS CLI, associate the VPC with the zone from the workload account, and then delete the authorization.
- Create a copy of the private hosted zone in the workload account, associate the copy with the workload VPC, and sync the records with a scheduled script.
- Replace the private hosted zone with a public hosted zone that has the same records, so that the workload VPC can resolve the names without an association.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Authorize the association from the shared-services account with the AWS CLI, associate the VPC with the zone from the workload account, and then delete the authorization.

**Deciding phrases.** "One VPC in a separate workload account", "the records must stay private", "cannot find the VPC", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** For a VPC of another account, [you first must authorize the association](../facts/route53.md#route53-cross-account-association-needs-authorization-no-console), and [you can't use the AWS console](../facts/route53.md#route53-cross-account-association-needs-authorization-no-console) for it, which is why the VPC is missing. [Using the account that created the hosted zone](../facts/route53.md#route53-cross-account-auth-by-hosted-zone-account), you authorize. [Using the account that created the VPC, associate](../facts/route53.md#route53-cross-account-auth-by-hosted-zone-account) the VPC with the zone.

**Why not.**

- "Create a VPC peering connection between a VPC ...": A private hosted zone will [only return these records when queried from within](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-private-zone-answers-only-from-associated-vpcs) associated VPCs, and peering associates nothing.
- "Create a copy of the private hosted zone ...": It works, but a second zone and a sync script are more to run than one association, and the two copies can drift apart.
- "Replace the private hosted zone with a public ...": A public hosted zone answers queries from anyone on the internet, which breaks the requirement that the records stay private.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the workload VPC is in the shared-services account" instead: associate the VPC in the console, because [you first must authorize the association](../facts/route53.md#route53-cross-account-association-needs-authorization-no-console) only for a VPC of another account.

**Takeaway.** A private hosted zone and a VPC in different accounts need an authorization, then an association, through the CLI or API.

**Review.** [A private hosted zone answers only through the VPC Resolver of its associated VPCs](2-deep.md#a-private-hosted-zone-answers-only-through-the-vpc-resolver-of-its-associated-vpcs-4-min)

</details>
